item.text: {"text":"[TiSASRec (2020)](https://jiachengli1995.github.io/files/wsdm20.pdf) remains the clearest foundation: attention incorporates absolute positions and pairwise historical time intervals, allowing equally spaced sequence positions to have different temporal relationships. Its attention mechanism is transferable as a design idea inside BERT4Rec without adopting the causal SASRec backbone. Recent related work includes [MSMT-LSI (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5), which uses multiple temporal embeddings and long/short-term attention, and a [BERT4Rec session-enhancement model (2026)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01554-z), which jointly learns content attention, continuous temporal decay and gated interest representations. These support investigating time-sensitive interest modeling; they do not establish gains on the pinned Amazon benchmark.\n\nPractical hypothesis: retain one bidirectional masked BERT4Rec per category and add a jointly learned, head-specific attention bias indexed by bucketed log historical time gaps. An optional nonnegative learned decay penalty can let some heads emphasize recent activity while others retain persistent interests. This is a proposed adaptation, not a verified result from these papers. For appended-mask inference, use the last observed timestamp as an explicit reference convention, or give mask-to-history edges a separate learned bias; neither requires the unknown next-event timestamp. Match that convention during training, keep targets masked, and avoid supplying held-out target timestamps. Compare with the established uniform control using fixed seeds, training budget and macro validation HR@10. Treat stale-interest reduction as a hypothesis: temporal proximity need not imply relevance, and strong decay may suppress useful older interests."}
